html:
The Southern Paiute are a Native American people of the Colorado River basin, in what is now southern Nevada, southern Utah and northern Arizona. They call themselves Nuwuvi. Their language, Colorado River Numic, belongs to the Uto-Aztecan family and is close to that of their neighbours the Ute.

They lived in small bands near springs and rivers, which is where the name Paiute is thought to come from: "paa" means water in Ute. Besides hunting and gathering, they farmed floodplains in spring with small reservoirs and ditches, growing corn, squash, beans and sunflowers.

The first Europeans to describe them were the Spanish friars of the Domínguez and Escalante expedition in 1776. In the 1800s slave raiders took Paiute women and children along the Old Spanish Trail to sell in New Mexico. From 1851 settlers of the Mormon church took over their best land and water. Disease and hunger followed. Today several bands hold small reservations, shown on the modern map as Nuwuvi lands, apart from their northern kin the Northern Paiute.
